scopes.report: The scope is the OIDC auth plugin: it checks a caller's bearer JWT against the identity provider's published key set (RS256/ES256 on ring, alg-confusion, crit and enc-key guards, exact issuer/audience with the azp rule, exp/nbf with skew, a fail-closed clock floor), turns the role claim into the principal's roles, keeps its own verdict cache that is flushed on refresh, and runs browser login (authorize URL, its own code-for-token exchange with the lent client secret, nonce binding, id_token verification). All of its I/O goes through the host connector over declared operator-infrastructure needs, as sans-IO single-flight fetches with refresh-ahead on tick. The verification logic, key-set caching and login flow hold up. The main gap is that the plugin's verify never names the credential line it consumes (it declares no carrier and returns no strip names), even though the locked auth-points rule says every auth called names its credential lines whatever its verdict. Today the kernel strips the bearer carriers itself, so no plane sees the token, but that relies on the kernel naming the line, which the same rule forbids. Smaller issues: the plugin writes identity bytes into the host's buffers before it knows they fit, against the short-buffer rule (and duplicates the SDK's one identity writer), and a stale doc comment says there is no driver ticket when the plugin's tick and drive use one. Read fully.

scopes.report: The crate is the inbound webhook-signature auth plugin: on the auth kind's verify, called once with the whole bounded body, it checks either a Twilio HMAC-SHA1 signature over the configured origin plus the received path and query (and, for POSTs, the sorted form parameters or a body digest carried in the signed URL) or a Standard Webhooks HMAC-SHA256 signature over id, timestamp and body within a timestamp tolerance. It answers pass when none of its headers are present, identity when a signature verifies, and reject otherwise (including a partial header set or a missing body), names all four signature header lines for stripping whatever the verdict, uses constant-time MAC comparison, holds its key in a zeroised buffer, and hands the kernel a Standard Webhooks replay key whose time-to-live is the rest of the tolerance window, while Twilio carries none, as the design rules. It holds no unsafe code, names no other plugin and keeps to the safe SDK door. The only defect is a wording one: the crate documentation says any request the host lent no body is refused, but a Twilio GET (the WebSocket upgrade case) is correctly judged on the URL alone without consulting the body. Read fully.
